title: The Turing test and its limits

sources.claim: Turing's 1950 paper "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" (Mind) proposed replacing "Can machines think?" with an imitation game in which an interrogator questions a hidden human and a machine; the test is debated, and the name is sometimes used loosely for any behavioral test.

sections.skill: Explain the imitation game and what passing would and would not show

questions.prompt: When did Turing publish "Computing Machinery and Intelligence"?

choices.text: 2022, the same year that chatbots first became widely available to the general public

questions.intro: In a 1950 paper, "Computing Machinery and Intelligence," Alan Turing suggested replacing the question "Can machines think?" with a test he called the IMITATION GAME. An interrogator exchanges typed messages with a hidden human and a hidden machine and tries to tell which is which. If the machine is hard to tell apart from the human, it does well. This is now often called the TURING TEST. It is debated: doing well shows a machine can produce human-like conversation, but whether that shows thinking or understanding is disputed.

questions.prompt: What does the interrogator try to do in the imitation game?

choices.text: Teach the machine to play chess against the human until one of them wins the game
Tell the hidden human from the machine

questions.correct_answer: Tell the hidden human from the machine

sections.skill: Compare the imitation game with a blind taste test

questions.prompt: In a blind taste test, what are you judging?

choices.text: Which drink has the most expensive bottle and the most attractive label in the store
Which drink is which, by taste

questions.correct_answer: Which drink is which, by taste
questions.intro: In a blind taste test, you taste two drinks without seeing labels and guess which is the famous brand. If you cannot tell, the other drink "passes." But passing shows only that it tastes similar to you, in that test. It does not show the ingredients are the same. The imitation game is similar: a machine that is hard to tell from a human in conversation has passed that test, but what that shows about thinking is debated.

sections.title: Apply it

questions.prompt: A machine passes by making typos and changing the subject. What does this show?

choices.text: That typos are the clearest possible proof that a machine understands what it is saying
That the judge is a machine

questions.intro: Several issues complicate the test. Results depend on the interrogator's skill and the time allowed; a short chat is easier to pass. Humans can be fooled by tricks such as jokes, typos or changing the subject. The name is also used loosely for any "seems human" impression, which is not Turing's setup. And a system could think in non-human ways and fail the test, or imitate well without understanding. These remain open questions.

questions.prompt: Someone says any chatbot that "seems human" passed the Turing test. What is wrong?

choices.text: Nothing, because any impression of seeming human is exactly what Turing described in 1950
